name: pH test strips, papers and meters
summary: Colour-change paper strips, or electronic meters with a glass probe, that show how acidic or alkaline a liquid is on the pH scale, where 7 is neutral.
uses: Tells acid from alkali: below 7 is acidic, above 7 alkaline (IGB cabbage); US rules call water-based waste corrosive at pH 2 or less, or 12.5 or more (40 CFR 261.22)
Shows whether water suits chlorine: disinfection works best below pH 8 (Health Canada chlorine TD)
pH never shows water is safe to drink: wells need separate tests for bacteria, nitrate and lead (Health Canada well test); drinking-water pH has no direct health effect (Health Canada pH TD)
Flags a strongly acid or alkaline liquid such as battery acid, wet cement or lye; a reading near 7 clears nothing else in it (acid and caustic hazard cards)
Acidic water dissolves more metal, so low-pH water through old pipes can carry more lead and copper (Health Canada pH TD)
Strips are only good to about half a colour step (Taylor FAQ); a meter is finer but only right if calibrated in fresh buffer (Health Canada pH TD; Hanna troubleshooting)
identify: Papers and strips come as a roll in a dispenser, a pad of strips, or plastic strips with one or more coloured pads, with a colour chart on the vial or dispenser. Hydrion prints the expiry date and lot number on the colour chart of every roll and dispenser (Hydrion help). Pool and spa kits test pH with drops of phenol red in a comparator, and the accepted range for pools and spas is 7.2 to 7.8, ideal 7.4 to 7.6 (Taylor FAQ). Chlorine above about 10 ppm can turn that test blue or purple and spoil the reading (Taylor FAQ). Meters are either a pen with a glass bulb at the tip under a cap, or a handheld box with a probe on a cable. Hanna says to keep the probe in storage solution when not in use, and never in distilled or deionised water, which damages it (Hanna troubleshooting; Hanna storage). Calibration buffers come in bottles marked pH 4.01, 7.01 and 10.01 (Hanna troubleshooting). Many meters also show mV and temperature and correct for temperature themselves (Hanna troubleshooting; Health Canada pH TD).
test: Strips and papers: 1. Read the expiry date on the colour chart; Hydrion gives its pH paper 3 years from manufacture if kept dry and out of direct sun (Hydrion help). 2. Check against known liquids: lemon juice should read well below 7 and baking soda in water above 7 (IGB cabbage). A strip that shows the same colour in both is no use. Meters: 1. Look at the bulb. A crack, or a meter that shows the same number in every buffer and sample, means the glass is broken (Hanna troubleshooting). 2. Soak a dry probe in storage solution for at least 2 to 3 hours (Hanna troubleshooting). 3. Calibrate in fresh pH 7.01 and 4.01 buffer (and 10.01 if you have it), rinsing with distilled water between them (Hanna troubleshooting). Opened pH 4.01 and 7.01 buffers keep 3 to 6 months; pH 10.01 only 1 to 3 months (Hanna troubleshooting). 4. If the meter has a mV mode: in pH 7.01 it should read within 30 mV of zero, and the change from 7.01 to 4.01 should be 150 to 186 mV (85 to 105% slope). If the offset is outside that, clean the probe; if the slope stays outside 85 to 105%, replace it (Hanna troubleshooting). 5. Don't trust a meter with no fresh buffer, or one that won't calibrate or never settles (Health Canada pH TD).

decay.note: Estimate. A meter probe lasts 1 to 2 years, less if stored in distilled water or used hot; opened buffers keep 3 to 6 months (Hanna troubleshooting). pH paper keeps 3 years from manufacture, dry and out of the sun (Hydrion help).

improvise: Red cabbage makes a usable indicator. Chop half a head, boil it in water for 10 minutes, cool and strain it. The purple liquid turns red at about pH 2, purple at 4, violet at 6, blue at 8, blue-green at 10 and greenish yellow at 12 (IGB cabbage). That is enough to tell a strong acid or a strong alkali from something near neutral, not to read tenths. A pool or spa kit's pH drops are another option (Taylor FAQ). For drinking water, pH is not the test that matters. A free-chlorine reading after treating clear water is: WHO says some free chlorine means the most dangerous organisms are gone and the water is likely safe, but chlorine does not remove chemicals and does not stop Cryptosporidium (WHO chlorine test; Health Canada chlorine TD). Health Canada says to test wells for bacteria, nitrate and lead separately (Health Canada well test). Useless or dangerous: tasting, sniffing closely or touching an unknown liquid to judge it. If it might be battery acid, lime, cement or lye, wear goggles and gloves and dip a strip, not a finger (acid and caustic hazard cards).
